title: How Does a Pastor Say No and Protect His Calling?
subtitle: Why every yes a pastor gives is a no to something else, and how learning to say no with conviction protects your focus, your calling, and the few things God actually asked of you.

sections.title: Every Yes Is a No
sections.body:
We talk about saying yes as if it were generosity and saying no as if it were stinginess. We have it exactly backward.

Every yes you give is a no you gave to something else without noticing. Say yes to the committee and you said no to the evening with your children. Say yes to the extra service and you said no to the sermon being ready. The yes is loud and visible and praised. The no is silent, paid by people who were not in the room when you decided.

I said yes to almost everything for the first decade of ministry. I thought it was faithfulness. It was fear. I could not bear to be the pastor who disappointed someone, so I disappointed the people I loved most and called it sacrifice. My calendar was full and my calling was starving and I could not tell the difference because both of them felt like work.

A leader who cannot say no does not actually decide anything. He simply accepts whatever the loudest request happens to be. His life is not chosen. It is assembled by other people, one yes at a time, and he wonders why it does not look like the thing he was called to.

sections.title: The Good Is the Enemy Here
sections.body:
It would be easy if the things competing for our yes were obviously bad. They are not. They are good. That is the whole problem.

The second small group is good. The denominational committee is good. The community event, the counseling overflow, the conference invitation, the new program someone is passionate about. None of them is sin. Each of them is a worthy thing that a serious Christian could give a life to. And that is precisely why they are dangerous. You can drown in good things. Most pastors do.

Jesus did not heal everyone. Read that slowly. There were sick people in towns he left and never returned to. There were crowds pressing in when he withdrew to a mountain to pray. He let good and urgent needs go unmet because he knew the difference between what was genuinely his to do and what merely presented itself. I have come out that I may preach, he said, and he moved on while needs remained.

If the sinless Son of God left good things undone to protect the few things he was sent for, your inability to do the same is not virtue. It is a failure to believe you have limits.

sections.title: Focus Is What You Owe Them
sections.body:
There is a fantasy that the best leader is the one available for everything. The opposite is true. The best leader is the one who has decided what he is for, and has the spine to protect it.

The apostles faced this directly. The widows were being overlooked, the complaint was legitimate, and the obvious move was for the twelve to handle it personally. They refused. It is not right that we should give up preaching the word of God to serve tables. That sentence has been read as arrogance for two thousand years. It was clarity. They knew what they were for, and they knew that doing the good thing in front of them would cost the essential thing behind it.

They did not abandon the widows. They built a structure so the widows would be served and the word would be preached. That is what focus looks like in practice. It is not neglect. It is the refusal to let the urgent eat the important, and the willingness to build something so the urgent gets handled by someone else.

Your congregation does not need you spread across forty things at half strength. They need you whole at the few things only you can do.

sections.title: How to Say It and Mean It
sections.body:
The no that protects your calling has to be a real no, not a maybe wearing a coat. The maybe is the cruelest answer. It keeps the other person hoping while it keeps you from committing, and it costs you the very energy the no was supposed to save.

Say it plainly. I am not able to take that on. No long apology, because the apology is usually you managing your own guilt at their expense. No false reason, because the lie will find you later. Just the truth, kindly delivered, and then silence while it lands.

Decide your noes before the requests come. A leader who decides in the moment decides badly, because in the moment the face in front of him is more real than the priorities behind him. Know your few things ahead of time. Know what your week protects and what your year is aimed at. Then most requests answer themselves before you ever sit down.

The goal is not to become a man who says no easily. The goal is to become a man whose yes means something because it is rare.

sections.title: Someone Will Be Disappointed
sections.body:
Here is the part no one tells you. There is no version of this where everyone is pleased with you. The choice is not between disappointing people and not disappointing people. The choice is only about which people.

Say yes to all of them and you disappoint your family, your soul, and the calling that brought you here. Learn to say no and you disappoint the person whose request you declined, who may not understand, who may carry it against you for a season. There is no door behind which everyone is satisfied. That door does not exist. The sooner you stop looking for it, the sooner you can lead.

The pastor who cannot bear to disappoint anyone ends up disappointing everyone slowly, including God, by giving a fraction of himself to everything and the whole of himself to nothing.

Decide who you are willing to disappoint. Then go disappoint them on purpose, for the sake of the few things that are actually yours to carry. That is not selfishness. That is the only way the essential thing survives.
